title: Bad Trips Guide, Round 26
intro: Round 26 (2026-11-08). What carries your round-24 versions, measured one thing at a time ([the results](https://github.com/u-dont-existDOTcom/joel-articles/blob/claude/bad-trips-20261105/articles/bad-trips/humanize/h33-20261108/RESULTS.md)). Your Give the Session without the Kenya story, the sitter joke and the redosing aside still reads Human, High ([its check](https://www.pangram.com/history/22506017-45a9-43c3-bcd2-ccb3c5732ed7)). Your anchor line and don'ts without the demon line still read Human, the don'ts at Medium ([its check](https://www.pangram.com/history/2a2e7aa4-5375-460b-8412-4480c5b5c3a5); the text starts with the first five minutes: that's the base each part is checked after, not a merge), so the demon line's break is what lifts them to High. My words in your frame read AI in all three tries on What Kind of Aftermath Is This?, the last written from a fresh reader's comparison of your Give the Session with my try ([its check](https://www.pangram.com/history/0ec38b6c-3395-42a6-b2ff-438096efe532), the paragraphs alone). So I stopped trying them and did what you asked first: say each thing once.

Two fresh readers read the stretches round 24 named against the whole guide ([What Kind of Aftermath Is This?](https://github.com/u-dont-existDOTcom/joel-articles/blob/claude/bad-trips-20261105/articles/bad-trips/humanize/h34-20261108/REPEATS-AFTERMATH.md), [the others](https://github.com/u-dont-existDOTcom/joel-articles/blob/claude/bad-trips-20261105/articles/bad-trips/humanize/h34-20261108/REPEATS-NAMED.md)). Most of what they found adds something no other line says (a remedy, a threshold, a script line), so it stays. Two lines only repeated what's said nearby and lose nothing, so they're gone: "Stabilize through sleep, food, routine, sober support, ordinary body, and ordinary world." (your After the Storm lines say it) and the Do list's "Offer choices instead of commands." (its own questions and your don'ts say it; [the rest of the reads](https://github.com/u-dont-existDOTcom/joel-articles/blob/claude/bad-trips-20261105/articles/bad-trips/humanize/h35-20261108/RESULTS.md)). And "Zendo-style" is explained where the guide first names it: "The Zendo Project, a harm-reduction group that offers peer support at festivals and other events to people having a hard time in an altered state, sums up its approach in four principles: ..."
Two cards, each a cut with a small downside.

suggestions.title: "A good sitter is not there to ..." said once
suggestions.what: The first sentence goes, so the section opens on the Zendo Project's four principles.
suggestions.why: Your anchor line and don'ts under Don't now say three of its four points: "win a philosophy debate" is your "don't try to win an argument with their visions ...", "impose an interpretation" is your "While many interpretations are possible ..." and "Don't force ... an insight on them", and "demonstrate spiritual advancement" is your "not the witch doctor guru who knows magic spells".
suggestions.stays: The Zendo sentence after it, and your anchor line and don'ts.
suggestions.deciding: Approve cuts the sentence; Reject keeps it as the section's first line.
suggestions.advice_note: Approve: it's the opening your new Don't section repeats.
suggestions.ask_because: downside: its fourth point, "perform a rescue fantasy" (the helper casting themselves as the hero who saves the person), is said nowhere else in the guide
suggestions.found_by: a fresh reader's read of what this paragraph's reader needs, after your round-24 versions went in

edits.before: A good sitter is not there to win a philosophy debate, perform a rescue fantasy, impose an interpretation, or demonstrate spiritual advancement. The Zendo Project, a harm-reduction group that offers peer support at festivals and other events to people having a hard time in an altered state, sums up its approach in four principles: creating a safe space, sitting with the person rather than guiding them, talking them through it rather than down from it, and remembering that difficult isn't necessarily bad.
edits.after: The Zendo Project, a harm-reduction group that offers peer support at festivals and other events to people having a hard time in an altered state, sums up its approach in four principles: creating a safe space, sitting with the person rather than guiding them, talking them through it rather than down from it, and remembering that difficult isn't necessarily bad.
